title: Translesion DNA synthesis on pyrimidine dimers by plant organellar DNA polymerases is metal-dependent.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Retrieved the Europe PMC full-text XML (194,120 characters, licence CC BY) and parsed it: it contains 11 figures, exactly 3 in-article tables and exactly one supplementary item, a single Word file named gkag707_supplemental_file.docx. I printed the tables: Table 1 is 10 oligonucleotide sequences, Table 2 is ~15 rows of exonuclease rate constants (k_obs in reciprocal seconds, with standard deviations, e.g. 0.035 +/- 0.01), Table 3 is a similarly small binding/rate table. I read the Results and Methods text. No accession numbers, no GEO/SRA/BioProject links, and a Zenodo/Dryad search on the DOI returned nothing.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The contents of the single .docx supplement: the Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out on both attempts (HEAD and GET at 120 s), so I could not open it. From the body text it is referenced only as 'Supplementary Fig. S1'-'S9' and never as a supplementary table, so it is almost certainly gel images and plots, not a data table. Bypass-efficiency percentages (75%, 62%, 85%, ~8-11%) are quoted in the text and plotted in figure panels; I did not see them as a column anywhere.

a1_downloadable.note: Article is CC BY and fully open; I downloaded the full-text XML and the three in-article tables. But there is no deposited dataset of any kind, and the one supplementary file (a .docx) would not download in two attempts.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. The quantity a model would predict - percent of primer extended past the lesion - exists only as bars in figure panels and numbers in prose. To get it as a column you would have to run densitometry on gel images or digitise plots by hand, i.e. construct the label.

a3_inputs_present.note: Table 1 gives the 10 DNA oligonucleotide sequences verbatim, and the two polymerase genes are named by Arabidopsis locus (At1g50840, At3g20540), so protein sequences are one UniProt lookup away. Inputs are not the problem.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are explicit and consistent in the tables I opened: k_obs in reciprocal seconds, enzyme and DNA concentrations in nanomolar, metal in millimolar, bypass as a percentage.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, by orders of magnitude. Table 2 holds ~15 measured rate constants; the whole study is roughly 7 enzyme variants x 3 DNA templates x 2 metal ions x a few concentrations, so on the order of tens to low hundreds of numbers. The checklist needs ~1,500 labelled rows, or ~400 for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small - the entire quantitative content is a few dozen numbers. Size was never the issue here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The text's claims (80-90% bypass of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, ~10% of 6-4 photoproducts, ~8-fold boost when exonuclease is silenced) are consistent with the Results narrative and tables I read; there are too few numbers for a count mismatch to arise.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels are genuine physical measurements - fluorescently labelled primer extension products separated on denaturing gels, quantified with ImageQuant, fitted in GraphPad Prism. No model output, no circularity. This is the one Part A item the paper does well.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model) would be the natural choice for polymerase sequence, with a DNA language model such as Nucleotide Transformer for the template strand
backbone.hardware: CPU laptop would suffice for the handful of sequences involved
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; irrelevant here because there is nothing to train on

integration.partner_dataset: UniProt (protein sequences and annotation) plus published translesion-synthesis bypass efficiencies for other polymerase families scattered across decades of biochemistry papers
integration.join_key: UniProt accession for the polymerase; lesion type as a controlled term
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could one predict how efficiently any DNA polymerase copies past a given ultraviolet-light lesion from its sequence alone? - a real question, but answering it needs a curated multi-paper compilation that does not exist, not this single eight-variant study.

controls.positive_control: Available in principle: T7 DNA polymerase, assayed here, is textbook-known to be blocked by both lesion types, and the paper confirms it - any model would have to reproduce that.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is runnable on any table, but with ~15 rows it carries no statistical weight.
controls.external_validation: None. The paper cites bypass efficiencies for T7 and E. coli polymerase I from other labs, but those are prose citations, not a joinable dataset.

honest_claim_h3: With these data a model could at best claim: 'across eight Arabidopsis organellar polymerase variants measured in one laboratory on one 49-nucleotide template, bypass efficiency tracks exonuclease activity and manganese substitution' - which is the paper's own conclusion, stated by the authors from the raw gels, and needs no model.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use DNA polymerase sequence and the type of ultraviolet damage to predict how often the enzyme copies past the damage.
plain_idea.train_on: What a model would see per example: the polymerase protein sequence (or which amino-acid insertion was deleted), the lesion in the template, which metal ion was supplied, and the enzyme concentration. Verified number of examples: roughly 15 tabulated rate constants plus a few dozen gel-derived percentages - far too few.
plain_idea.predict: Percent of primer extended past the lesion, or the exonuclease rate constant in reciprocal seconds. The true answer comes from fluorescently labelled primer extension on denaturing polyacrylamide gels, band intensities measured in ImageQuant and fitted in GraphPad Prism.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Plant and mitochondrial genome-stability researchers would like to know which polymerase features permit lesion bypass, but this study was designed to test a mechanism in one enzyme pair, not to train anything.

ml_idea: The only sensible machine-learning framing - predict translesion-synthesis bypass efficiency from polymerase sequence and lesion chemistry - would require a curated compilation of such measurements across many polymerase families and many labs. This paper contributes roughly eight enzyme variants to that hypothetical compilation. It is a potential future data point, not a project.

effort.compute_note: No estimates given for embedding or cross-validation because there is no dataset to run them on; the working-set figure is the measured size of the full-text XML plus its three small tables.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in the article's tables. I did: Table 2 has ~15 measured rate constants and the single supplementary file is a Word document of gel figures. That is the whole quantitative dataset, and it kills the project in one step.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A on two killers, both verified in the retrieved full-text XML rather than inferred from the abstract. A2: the prediction target, percent bypass past an ultraviolet lesion, appears only as bars in gel-quantification figures and numbers in prose, so it would have to be reconstructed by densitometry. A5: the entire quantitative output is ~15 tabulated rate constants plus a few dozen figure-only percentages from eight enzyme variants on one 49-nucleotide template, against a threshold of ~1,500 rows. The science is clean and the labels are honest physical measurements (A8 passes cleanly), but this is a mechanistic biochemistry paper with no dataset, no repository deposit and no accessions - there is nothing to model.
